title: Scholz–Brauer conjecture
formal: For every positive integer n, is \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell (n)\), where \(\ell\)\((m)\) is the minimum length of an addition chain for m?
why: The conjecture predicts a precise relationship between optimal multiplication plans for an exponent and for its associated all-ones binary integer. Its restricted-chain theorem shows that the unresolved issue concerns how the freedom to reuse older values affects the best possible length.

progress.text: Brauer proves the inequality for the minimum star-chain length ℓ*, as recorded in Wallner’s Section 7.
Tall, Theorems 2–4, proves the conjecture for a specified infinite family with seven binary ones and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and for its doubles.
Wallner states the unrestricted Scholz–Brauer inequality among open addition-chain problems and distinguishes the star-chain result.
Agama’s preprint claims asymptotic density one and explicitly leaves the uniform all-integers version unanswered; not independently proof-audited.
Agama’s later preprint abstract claims the inequality for integers with an optimal chain in its quasi-closed class; abstract-only review.

definitions: For a positive integer m, an addition chain of length r is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers \(1=a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots <a_{r}=m\) such that, for each \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,r\}\), there exist \(j,k\in \{0,\ldots ,i- 1\}\) with \(a_{i}=a_{j}+a_{k}\). The indices j and k may coincide, and any previously produced value may be reused any number of times. The length counts the r additions, excluding the initial 1. Define \(\ell\)\((m)\) as the minimum such r; this minimum exists because \(1,2,\ldots ,m\) is an allowed chain, and \(\ell\)\((1)=0\). Only additions of two previously available numbers are allowed: subtraction, division, arbitrary preloaded constants and sums of three or more terms in one step are excluded. All additions have cost one, regardless of operand size; this is an operation-count question, not a bit-running-time bound. A star chain, also called a Brauer chain, additionally requires each step to have a representation \(a_{i}=a_{i- 1}+a_{j}\) with \(j<i\). Write \(\ell\)*\((m)\) for its minimum length. Thus \(\ell\)\((m)\le \ell *(m)\); the conjecture uses the unrestricted \(\ell\) on both sides. The integer \(2^{n}- 1\) has n ones in binary, and the quantifier includes \(n=1\).
answer_criterion: Prove the inequality for every positive integer n, or give an integer n together with rigorous bounds on the two minimum lengths showing \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)>n- 1+\ell (n)\). A positive proof may establish existence of the required chains without an efficient algorithm for finding a shortest chain. Equality is not required. Restricted-chain results, a finite verification range, and validity for a density-one set of integers are weaker than the universal assertion.

context_blocks.text: An addition chain is a plan for reusing intermediate powers. Once \(x^{a}\) and \(x^{b}\) have been computed, one multiplication produces \(x^{a+b}\). Starting from x, a chain for m therefore specifies a multiplication-only computation of \(x^{m}\) with one multiplication per chain step. This correspondence explains the interest in short chains; it does not include algorithms that use division or other algebraic operations.

For \(n=5\), the chain 1,2,4,5 has length three and is shortest, since two additions can reach at most four. The conjectured upper bound for \(2^{5}- 1=31\) is therefore \(5- 1+3=7\). The chain 1,2,3,6,12,24,30,31 attains that upper bound: its last two additions are \(24+6\) and \(30+1\). Exhibiting it checks this instance without claiming that every n admits an analogous optimal pattern.

The target compares the cost of building an integer n with the cost of building a much larger integer whose binary expansion is entirely ones. Its dominant term is \(n- 1\), with only \(\ell\)\((n)\) further additions allowed. Merely finding a chain of order n steps would leave the exact additive allowance unresolved.

Brauer’s theorem gives \(\ell\)*\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell *(n)\). In a star chain, every step must use the immediately preceding value. This proves the desired inequality whenever n has a shortest unrestricted chain that is also a star chain. In general, replacing \(\ell\)*\((n)\) by the potentially smaller \(\ell\)\((n)\) is precisely the distinction that the restricted result does not settle.

Tall’s 2024 paper proves the conjecture for an explicit infinite family of integers with seven ones in binary and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and also for their doubles. An infinite family need not cover all possible exponents; its role here is a proved special case, rather than a resolution of the universal target.

A May 2026 preprint claims that the proportion of \(n\le N\) satisfying the conjecture tends to one as N tends to infinity. Its introduction expressly distinguishes this claim from a proof for all n. Even a valid density-one theorem can leave exceptions, and this preprint’s proof has not been independently verified in this review.

There is no contradiction in a chain for \(2^{n}- 1\) being shorter than the displayed bound: the conjecture is an upper bound. Nor must a positive solution provide a fast procedure for computing \(\ell\)\((n)\). These distinctions keep an existence inequality separate from exact-length formulas and shortest-chain optimization.

sentences: An addition chain starts at one and builds its target by repeatedly adding two already available values.
Its length counts additions and corresponds to the number of multiplications in the associated repeated-power computation.
The conjecture asks whether the minimum length for \(2^{n}- 1\) is always at most \(n- 1\) plus the minimum length for n.
The analogous theorem for star chains and known infinite families leave the unrestricted universal inequality open in the checked sources.
Resolving it would explain how efficiently optimal exponentiation plans can control the cost of all-ones binary exponents.
